Weed and tidy front garden beds

lessons.bigIdea: A hallucination is when the AI states something false in a confident voice. It's like a mate at the pub who'd rather give you a smooth answer than admit he doesn't know. The AI is predicting words that sound right, not checking facts, so a made-up name, quote or number can look just as polished as a real one.
lessons.useCase: You ask for stats to back up an IdenGap post and it hands you a neat "study" with a percentage. Before you use it, ask for the source, then check the source yourself. If it can't point to a real one, treat the number as made up.
lessons.proTip: Tell it up front: "If you're not sure, say so. Don't guess." Then for anything that matters (numbers, quotes, names, dates), verify it yourself before it goes out.

lessons.bigIdea: A context window is how much the AI can keep in mind at once, like a whiteboard in a meeting room. Everything you've said in the chat, plus what you've pasted in, goes on the board. When it fills up, the oldest stuff gets wiped to make room, so in a long chat it can quietly forget what you told it at the start.
lessons.useCase: Someone pastes a 40-page contract and asks for the risky bits. That works because it all fits on the board. But after an hour of back and forth on something else, asking "what was clause 12 again?" might get a wrong answer, because the contract has started to drop off.
lessons.proTip: For anything important, start a fresh chat and put the key info right at the top. If a long chat starts going off track, ask it "summarise what we've agreed so far in 5 lines", then paste that summary into a new chat and carry on from there.

lessons.bigIdea: An LLM is like a new apprentice who's read a lot, but doesn't know what you want until you say it clearly. A vague ask gets a vague result. A good prompt names the job, who it's for, the tone, and what "done" looks like, like giving a clear brief instead of "can you sort this".
lessons.useCase: Instead of "write a post about habits", try: "Write a 6-line X post for tired dads who keep starting over. Direct, no fluff, no hashtags. Start with the feeling, then the small action." That's the difference between a generic post and one you can actually use.
lessons.proTip: Use this shape every time: Role + Task + Audience + Constraints. "You're an IdenGap coach. Write 3 short options for a caption about starting small. Audience is working dads. No jargon, no emoji, under 400 characters."

lessons.bigIdea: An LLM is a very well-read autocomplete. It has read a huge amount of text, and all it does is predict the next word that fits, again and again. It doesn't look facts up or "know" things the way you do. It's spotted the patterns in how people write and explain things.
lessons.useCase: A tradie says "write a quote email for a deck job, friendly, under 100 words", and the LLM writes something that sounds like thousands of good quote emails it's seen. A coach pastes in rough notes and gets a clean session summary back. In both cases it's matching patterns, not thinking up something new.
lessons.proTip: It answers in the style you set it up for, so give it a role and an audience. Instead of "explain habits", try: "You're a coach talking to a tired dad who works labouring jobs. Explain in 5 short lines why small habits change identity." The answer will be a lot sharper.
